before: Your little one wants to play, too, which is why I call the deeper therapy pl/ork, play + work. A lot of the best discoveries come when you're both just messing around, kind of like how kids tell you what's really going on from the back seat, when nobody's looking right at them. Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured.

guide_passage: The cynical voice, numbness, urge to scroll, anger, dissociation, or sudden need to do something else all belong inside the pl/ork. The response may be a protector, the child speaking directly, an inherited critic, a present-day grievance, or a blend. Start with what it is trying to prevent, accomplish, or communicate before deciding who is speaking.
next: Sometimes it is only a thought. Do not create a new inner person every time the mind produces a sentence. Use the least elaborate model that helps. A thought can be labeled “thinking,” allowed to pass, and followed by a return to the room. If it keeps returning with a coherent fear, strategy, age, or demand, a parts dialogue may help. The model serves the person, not the other way around.
length: two to four sentences, 50 to 90 words
brief:
- the first paragraph after Joel's pl/ork paragraph (which ends "Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured."), under the heading "Start With Whatever Showed Up".
- what it has to carry, in meaning: you go looking for your little one and get something else (you get mad, or you zone out and realize you've been staring at the rug); that counts as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before deciding where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or get, or say. It could be any of these, or a mix: your little one (maybe mad you took so long to come back), a part of you that's trying to protect you (Joel, 22:44: "i agree to add that part of you trying to protect you"), the parent you inherited, or something actually going on in your life now (not only something from earlier today: a partner who keeps hurting you or a job grinding you down counts too).
- The last version ended on one long sentence listing all of those, right after the sentence with the three questions, and Pangram flagged those last two sentences (66% AI). Don't end on a list, and don't put the questions and the sources back to back as two lists. Say them the way the narrator would out loud.
- The article already has, at the start of this h1: "you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone, dinner, or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly". Don't repeat that list.
- Joel, 2026-10-02 22:44: the protective part is "the inherited protector that came from trauma responses", not "the adult protector, which is the one we are consciously building". Never call it "the Protector".
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything sections back; core terms (your little one, the Nurturer, the Protector, the Guide, the inherited critic voice, borrowed adulthood, pl/ork) are fine.
